At is particularly difficult to begin this second column to you
because of the recent death of Robert W. Morey, Pi '20,
former President ofthe Executive Council. Bob died peace
fully on July 9, 1985, at his home in Short Hills, New Jersey,
at the age of 87. His service to Psi U will, of course, be
remembered by all with whom he came in contact. His zest
for life and his positive approach to brotherhood made him
always approachable and an undying songster to the end.
While many tributes will be paid to Bob in the months and
years that lie ahead, none will be as important to him as the
knowledge that the Fraternity continues to grow and provide
the continuing opportunity for young men and women to
expand their college experience beyond the normal
academic environment that an undergraduate might other
wise have.
One of the events that Bob most treasured attending
annually was the Convention! Our 142nd Convention will be
held from August 28-31st in Champaign, Ilhnois with the
Omicron Chapter. This year we will be trying some new
ideas for the Convention, including providing a general
theme. Since we have just finished celebrating the 150th
anniversary of the founding of the Fraternity, it is appropri
ate that this year our attention should be drawn to the history
and traditions ofthe Fraternity. We are particularly excited
about the Sesquicentennial History of the Fratemity that is
being written by Brother Travis Jacobs, son ofthe writer of
the Annals of Psi Upsilon and grandson of the writer of the
original history of the Fraternity. Our history provides us
with many lessons that can be helpful to us today not only in
fashioning modern fraternity education programs but in de
veloping enhanced rituals that reflect the original goals ofour
founders. We hope to focus on these themes at the Conven
tion this year to encourage a rebirth of interest in our history
and to remind us that many ofthe problems that we
experi
ence today have occurred before and can be solved using
approaches that served our earlier brothers well. The Con
vention will also see the initial establishment of the first
Alumni Advisory Board, which was authorized by last year's
Convention. Having the assistance of an alumnus from each
Chapter who can attend the annual Convention and provide
the International Fratemity with the benefit of local alumni
experience will enhance our ability to develop new lead
ership for the International Fraternity. Finally, the Conven
tion will, of course, serve as the business meeting of the
Fratemity and will consider matters ranging from Constitu
tional amendments to the budget of the Fraternity for 19851986. Join us!
Probably the best news that we have had in recent years is
that we ended the fiscal year on June 30, 1985, in the black!
This success is due in no small measure to the overwhelming
support provided by our alumni during the Annual Giving
Program. We had set a goal of $135,000 this year for the
Annual Giving Program and exceeded that goal by almost
$7,000. All of us who are involved in leading the Fraternity
are grateful to the more than 2,000 alumni who participated
in making this year's Program such a success!
I unveiled at the June meeting of the Executive Commit
tee a new 1985-1986 Psi Upsilon Management Improvement
Program that will assist us in planning for the events of each
Psi U year somewhat further in advance than we have been
able to do in the past. I hope that this program will allow us to
inaugurate "The Fowrf/i Fifty Years: A Beginning." This
(1) Build a financially sound Fratemity, beginning with the
budget for fiscal year 1985-1986, including providing for a
reasonable cash flow for the Fraternity;
(2) Restructure the Convention, Divisional Conferences,
and the Undergraduate and Alumni Advisory Boards to
assure a timely and useful theme for each type of meeting
with an identified date and time for each meeting announced
at the Convention each year for the entire year so individual
members can adequately plan for their attendance at these
meetings;
(3) Increase ,the number of Executive Council meetings
firom four to six and eliminate separate Executive Committee
meetings, in recognition ofthe reduced size ofthe Executive
Council and the increased participation by its members;
(4) Creation ofa Task Force on Ritual to provide a Fraterni
ty-wide series of rituals that can be used for pledging cere
monies, pre-initiation and initiation ceremonies, as well as in
conjunction with Chapter meetings and alumni gatherings,
and that will provide a significant contribution to the
Fratemity Education Program for new pledges; and
(5) Increase emphasis on the history of the Fraternity as a
critical part ofthe Fratemity Education Program for brothers
and pledges alike.
The death of Bob Morey represents the passing of a great
generation of Psi U's. That passing also gives us an opportu
nity for a new beginning. The story of our Fratemity is the
story of constant change as one new generation of under
graduates is succeeded by the next. The strength ofcharacter
and spirit embodied in a Psi U like Bob Morey is the constant
that we hope will allow us to continue, to improve what is
good, and to try new ideas that will lead us into the future. I
look forward to your help as we continue in Bob Morey's
footsteps.
Yours in the Bonds,
William R . Robie
President
Epsilon Omega '66

NEW FOUNDATION PRESIDENT
(New York, NY) On April 16, Robert L.
Kaiser, Zeta '30, was elected as President
of The Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc. He
succeeds Robert A. McDowell, Pi '40,
who has served admirably for the past two
years in this capacity. During his tenure,
the Sesquicentennial Fund Drive saw
real progress, and Foundation support to
the Fraternity grew by leaps and bounds.
We can only hope that he is merely step
ping down �
not out! But Brother
McDowell could not turn over the reins
to a better qualified individual. Bob Kai
ser has been a Director ofthe Foundation
since 1983, a member of the Executive
Council since 1978, and Vice President of
the Council since 1982. His commitment
to Psi Upsilon is further demonstrated by
his devotion and loyalty to the Zeta Chap
ter. As faculty advisor to the Chapter and
secretary of the alumni association since
1965, Brother Kaiser (as well as his wife
Evelyn, Zeta '83H) has provided unpar
alleled guidance and assistance to both
undergraduates and alumni. Brother
Kaiser directs Dartmouth's Bequest and
Estate Planning Program, which is wide
ly regarded as one of the most successful
planned giving programs in the country.
Brother Kaiser is truly the ideal person to
succeed Bob McDowell. To Brother
McDowell we utter a grateful thank you,
and to Brother Kaiser, a fervent wish for
the best of luck in his new position!

rlobert W. Morey, Pi '20, former Presi
dent of the Executive Council, died on
July 9, 1985 at his home in Short Hills,
New Jersey. He was 87 years old.
Brother Morey was the quintessential
Psi U. He was loved by all who knew him
and was often heard to remark, "I never
met a Psi U I didn't like." His contribu
tions to the Fraternity, both in terms of
concrete accomplishments and goodwill
generated, are truly countless. His death
represents a tragic loss to the Fraternity
and to all who knew him.
Born in Meadville, Pennsylvania and
raised in Pittsburgh, Bob Morey at
tended Shadyside Academy before
entering Syracuse University, where his
lifetime commitment to Psi Upsilon be
gan when he was initiated into the Pi
Chapter in March of 1917. His college
career was interrupted by World War I,
during which he served in the United
States Navy. But he returned to Syracuse
after the war and graduated in 1920 with a
Bachelor of Arts degree. Subsequently,
he attended the Graduate School ofBank
ing at Rutgers University.
Brother Morey had an impressive busi
ness career which began in 1920 when he
entered the training program of Swift &
Co. in Chicago. After two years he be
came manager of the Cleveland office of
the Guaranty Company of New York,
where he remained for twelve years. In
1934 he joined the C. F. Childs Company
in Cleveland as Assistant Vice President,
where his primary responsibility was
dealing with United States Government
Securities.
Joining the Morgan Guaranty Trust
Company of New York in 1938, Brother
Morey served as Vice President of the
Banking Department, from 1940-58 of
the New England Division and from
1958-63 of the Metropolitan New York
Division. Upon his retirement at age 65,
he joined the Witco Chemical Corpora
tion in New York City as a consultant, in
which capacity he continued for another
twenty years, commuting daily from his
home in Short Hills to the city which he
found so exciting and stimulating.
Bob Morey was a multi-dimensional
man with a wide variety of interests
beyond his family and business career.
Certainly one ofhis primary interests was
Syracuse University. He served his alma
mater as President of the Cleveland
Alumni Association, Chairman of the
Building and Development Fund of the
New York Metropolitan Association,
member of the Administrative Board of
Athletics, Chairman ofthe Annual Alum
ni Fund, President of the New York
Alumni Association, and as a Trustee. In
1964 he was honored with the Syracuse
University Alumni Award, the highest
honor which Syracuse bestows upon an
alumnus, for his years of dedication and
service.
Norwich University also benefitted
from Brother Morey's interest and exper
tise. From 1954-73 he was a Trustee of
this institution and chairman of its Fi
nance Committee. He was awarded an
honorary Doctor of Laws degree from
Norwich in 1969.
At last year's Convention at the Eta
Chapter, Bob Morey played an impor
tant role in leading the memorial ser
vice. Brother Morey regularly was
called upon to speak at Psi U functions,
for no one did so with more feeling.
Bob Morey's involvement in Psi Upsilon
was all-consuming, and it was a rare
Fraternity event that he missed. The pic
ture above was taken at the New York
Founders' Day dinner last November,
where he honored his successor as Presi
dent of the Executive Council upon his
retirement.
Bob Morey also served as a director of
the Vermont Marble Company and ofthe
Pond Lily Company. Very active in
Christ Church of Short Hills, he became
its Treasurer in 1967 and continued in
that post for many years thereafter. Con
sistent with his consuming interest in
youth and education, he served for years
as a Trustee of the Japan Intemational
Christian University Foundation.
Of all Bob Morey's interests, though,
none was more important to him than his
activity in Psi Upsilon. His own fratemity
experience at the Pi Chapter was ex
ceedingly rewarding to him, and he
wanted to assure that future generations
of young people would have the oppor
tunity to experience what he considered
this invaluable adjunct to a college educa
tion.
Brother Morey became a member of
the Executive Council in 1967, was
elected as its Vice President six months
later, and became its 15th President in
1973. He served in the latter capacity
until 1979 and as a life member of the
Executive Council thereafter.
During his tenure as President of the
Fraternity's administrative body. Bob
Morey oversaw the balancing of Psi Up-

silon's budget after years of deficit spend
ing, the successful reactivation ofthe Rho
and Epsilon Phi Chapters, the moving of
the Psi Upsilon office from Ann Arbor,
Michigan to Paoli, Pennsylvania, the
birth and refinement of the Field Direc
tor program, the computerization of the
Fraternity's records, the dramatic growth
of the Annual Giving program, and the
assumption of a leadership role in the
interfraternity movement.
Psi Upsilon took giant strides during
Bob Morey's term as President, but his
most valuable and lasting contribution to
the Fraternity is one that cannot be
documented or measured. He gave us
himself�
his genuine concern for others,
his affable nature, his ability to interact
with people of all ages, his positive out
look on life, and his sincere understand
ing and appreciation of young people.
Wherever he went and with whomever
he spoke. Bob Morey left behind a feeling
of goodwill.
One might assume that Brother
Morey's activity in Psi Upsilon dimin
ished upon his "retirement" as President
of the Executive Council, but nothing
could be farther from the truth. He con
tinued to attend every Executive Council
meeting. Founders' Day dinner, and
Convention that was humanly possible.
Just two weeks before his death he was in
Paoli at the Fraternity office for a meeting
of the Executive Committee, and his
thoughtful comments, observations, and
suggestions were just as meaningful as
ever.
In addition to his Executive Council
responsibilities. Bob Morey was a direc
tor of The Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc.
from 1974 until his death. He served as
President of this body from 1980-82 and
as Chairman of the Board thereafter. He
was among the forward-thinking indi
viduals who assisted in converting the
Foundation from a private to a public
entity, thereby providing it with greater
latitude in effectively directing its funds
to the long-range operations of the
Fraternity.
Bob Morey is survived by his wife of
almost 58 years, the former Elizabeth
Brahm, and by his two children, Louise
Severance ofChappaqua, New York, and
Robert W. Morey, Jr. of San Francisco,
California. He also left behind nine
grandchildren. It was one of Brother
Morey's greatest joys that two of his
grandchildren became members of Psi
Upsilon: Laurie Severance, Kappa '83,
and Robert W. Morey, III, Pi '86.
In keeping with Brother Morey's abid
ing interest in youth and education, the
Morey family has requested that, in lieu
of flowers, contributions be made to the
Psi Upsilon Foundation Scholarship
Fund, Two Station Square, Paoh, PA
19301. Starting next year, the Robert W.
Morey, Pi '20 Award will be granted to at
least one highly qualified undergraduate.
Nothing would have pleased Bob Morey
more than to know that he was helping to
educate the young people whom he loved
so dearly.
Bob Morey was a very special indi
vidual. He was just as comfortable dis
cussing the stock market with a con
temporary as in "downing a brew" with a
new initiate. And never was he happier
than when crooning his favorite Psi U
songs. He will be sorely missed, but he
left behind a legacy which will endure
forever.

An Expression of Gratitude
from Psi Upsilon Fraternity to
ROBERT WILLIS MOREY, Pi '20
upon His Retirement as
Fifteenth President of the Executive Council
VV hen your name was
proposed for membership on the Executive Council in
May 1967, all present were assured that "by adding him to our Council we
would be doing an
outstanding service
to the Fraternity.
"
Twelve years later fhundreds of Psi Upsilon alumni and f
undergraduates can attest to the
generous fulfillment of that predic
tion.
You brought to the Executive
Council a wealth of experience and
wisdom gained from a
distinguished
banking career, including twenty-five
years as a vice president ofthe Morgan
Guaranty Trust Company of New
York. Education always has been im
portant to you, for you served Syra
cuse
University in many alumni capac
ities, among these as a trustee for six
years. You were a trustee of Norwich
University for twenty-two years and
have been a member ofthe Executive
Committee of the Japan International Christian University Foundation for the
last thirteen years. It is little wonder that your Alma Mater honored you with its
Alumni Award in 1964 and Norwich University with a Doctor of Laws degree in
1969.
Psi Upsilon recognized your talents quickly. Within six months ofyour joining
the Executive Council you were elected a vice president, serving in this office
for six years, until you were chosen to lead as the fifteenth president in 1973.
One year later you were elected to the Board of Directors of The Psi Upsilon
Foundation, Inc. Now you have asked to be relieved of your principal responsi
bilities after a term of office exceeded in length by only four other presidents in
nearly a century and a haff.
In the last six years you have been instrumental in leading our beloved
Fratemity to many signal achievements. As fraternities across the land have
regained stature and strength, you have overseen a dramatic increase in mem
bership and a return to perhaps the healthiest condition most of our Chapters
ever have known. You have restored the Fraternity's financial operations to a
balanced budget and have influenced the reactivation of two Chapters and the
founding of one new provisional Chapter. Not least among your accomplish
ments has been the gradual revival of many great traditions, notably an enthu
siasm for delving into Psi Upsilon's vast and unique treasury of songs.
But it is the man we are honoring on this occasion, a brother whose character
and personality transcend even his achievements. One whom we profoundly
admire and respect as a gentleman and genuine friend, you are an example to all
in our Fraternity whose lives you have touched. We have found you dedicated in
your efforts, determined in your objectives, and tireless in your energies. Eager
to visit one more Chapter on a moment's notice, your warm congeniality glows
brightest with a toast in your hand and a song on you lips.
You may be stepping down, but you can never step out of our circle of
brotherly love and affection. We salute you; we thank you; and we extend our
heartfelt good wishes for many more years of good health and close bonds in Psi
Upsilon.
Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39
Executive Vice President

Jiiach year the Fraternity staff and the
Chapter which has been chosen to host
the current Convention begin the plan
ning for this annual event with the hope
that it will be the best ever. Facilities
must be secured, menus determined, so
cial events planned, speakers arranged, a
suitable memento ordered, business
agenda determined, a photographer con
tracted, delegate materials prepared �
the details seem endless. And there are
times when it looks like it will never come
together.
But once again all the pieces have fallen
into place, and the 1985 Convention has
shaped up into what we hope will be a
truly memorable occasion. All in Psi Up
silon are cordially invited to attend the
142nd Convention of the Fraternity,
hosted this year by the Omicron Chapter
at the University of Illinois in Champaign
in commemoration of its seventy-fifth
anniversary, from Wednesday, August
28, through Saturday, August 31.
"Building a Future on Tradition" will
be an appropriate theme as we chart the
course for tomorrow based upon our
strong history and long-held beliefs and
traditions. Various workshops and semi
nars will emphasize the value of our sim
ple but effective rituals, which have
proven through the years to be timeless
and enduring. In keeping with this em
phasis on ritual. Convention participants
will have the opportunity to attend the
dignified initiation ceremony of the
Omicron Chapter and a fitting memorial
service to honor those in Psi U who have
gone before us.
Business sessions will include general
meetings, an Executive Council meeting,
divisional conferences, workshops, and
seminars. Of particular interest will be a
special presentation by David L. Westol,
Assistant Prosecuting Attorney for Kala
mazoo County.
Although the primary purpose of the
Convention is to act as Psi Upsilon's leg-

islative body, there is no shortage ofsocial

lectable viands. The highlight ofany Con

us on

vention banquet, which will be preceded

brotherhood and fine fellowship will be at
its highest on this festive evening, which

good times.

place at the University Inn, a luxurious

home" for attendees.

ably chaired by Bob Mclntire, Omicron
'68, and the Fraternity staff have been
hard at work planning what they hope will
